lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Good afternoon, Larkfield Garden Centre, Neil speaking. How can I help?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Oh, hi. I'm calling about the part-time job you advertised in the local paper last week. Is it still available?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: It is, yes. We haven't filled it yet. Can I take your name first?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: It's Amy Clarke. I'm a student at the college in town, so I'm really looking for something at weekends.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Right, well, that should suit you nicely. What do you know about the job so far?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Not much, to be honest. The advert just said general assistant. I was hoping it might be in the café, because I've done a bit of waitressing before.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Ah, I'm afraid the café jobs all went at Easter. This one's in our garden furniture section, so tables, chairs, benches, parasols, that kind of thing. You'd be helping customers, keeping the displays tidy and arranging home deliveries.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Oh, that sounds fine. I don't mind at all, really. And which days would it be?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Every Saturday, from nine till five. Then we'd want you every other Sunday as well. We did think about asking for Friday evenings too, but we've got enough people for those now.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Every other Sunday is no problem. My lectures are all on weekdays anyway. Can I ask about the pay?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Sure. Everyone starts on 12 pounds an hour. Once you've finished your three-month trial period, it goes up to 13.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: That's better than I expected, actually.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Good. Now, there are a few practical things. We give you a company fleece and a pair of gloves, because some of the furniture's heavy and the edges can be quite rough.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Do I need to wear anything in particular?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Yes, you'll need your own boots, the kind with a hard toe. We can't supply those, I'm afraid, because everyone's a different size. And ordinary trainers aren't allowed on the shop floor.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: That's okay. I've got a pair from a summer job I did on a farm.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Perfect. And before you start, there's some training. Everyone does a half-day course with our health and safety officer. It's mostly about lifting, so how to move heavy items without hurting your back. You'd be surprised how many people injure themselves with a stone bench.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: I can imagine. I'm happy to do that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: So, Amy, would you like to come in for an interview?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Yes, please, that would be great.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: We're interviewing next week. How about Tuesday the 12th of May, in the afternoon?

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Ah, I've got an exam that day. Is there any chance of a different day?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Let me see. What about Thursday the 14th? Same time, two o'clock.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Yes, Thursday the 14th is perfect.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Great. You won't be seeing me, though. The interviews are done by our assistant manager, Clare Whitlock.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Sorry, how do you spell her surname?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: It's W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K. Just ask for her at the main desk when you arrive.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Okay. Should I bring anything with me?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: We'll need to see some proof of identity. A student card isn't enough, unfortunately. It has to be your passport. You don't need to bring a CV, though, because you'll fill in a form on the day.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Fine. Oh, and I'll probably cycle over. Is there anywhere to leave a bike?

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: There is. A lot of people look for it by the main entrance, but we moved the bike rack last year. It's now right next to the greenhouse, at the back of the car park.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: Great. And one last thing. Is there a staff discount? My mum's a keen gardener, so she'll definitely want to know.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Ha, everyone asks that. Staff get 20 percent off anything in the shop. It used to be 15, but we increased it in January. It doesn't apply in the café, though, because that's run by a separate company.

lines.speaker: caller
lines.text: She'll be pleased. Thanks very much, Neil. I'll see Clare on Thursday, then.

lines.speaker: manager
lines.text: Good luck, Amy. Bye now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.text: Part 2. You will hear a tour guide talking to a group of visitors about a day trip on a heritage railway. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Morning, everyone, and welcome aboard. My name's Callum, and I'll be your guide for today's trip on the Ashcombe Valley Railway. We'll be at the station in about twenty minutes, so I thought I'd use the time to tell you how the day's going to work.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: First, a little background. The railway opened in 1868 to carry slate from the quarries down to the coast. It closed in the 1960s, like so many small lines, but a group of volunteers bought the track and spent nearly thirty years restoring it. Today the trains are all pulled by steam engines, and almost everyone you'll meet working on the line is still a volunteer.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Right, a quick word about what your ticket covers, because I always get asked. Some of you have been wondering about lunch. There is a dining car on the train, and the food's very good, but it isn't part of the package, so you'll need to pay for that yourselves on board. Or you can do what a lot of people do and bring a picnic.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: What is included is entry to the railway museum at Ashcombe station, which has a lovely collection of old engines and signalling equipment. Just show your wristband at the door. You'll also notice a guidebook for sale in the station shop. It's five pounds, and it's well worth it, but again, that's up to you.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Now, I know a few of you were hoping to ride on the footplate, up in the cab with the driver. Unfortunately, those places are booked months in advance, so that won't be possible today. But here's the good news. When we reach the far end of the line, afternoon tea is waiting for you in the old waiting room at Hartfield, and that's all been paid for. There'll be scones, sandwiches and a very large pot of tea.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Next, a bit of advice for the journey itself. When you get on, most people head straight for the seats on the right-hand side, because that's where the river is as you leave the station. But the river disappears after about five minutes, and from then on all the best views of the valley are on the left. So if you want good photos, sit on the left.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: These are the original carriages, so the windows open. You just pull the leather strap and the window drops down. That's lovely on a warm day, but there are two tunnels on the line, and if the window's open when we go into one, the whole carriage fills with smoke and soot. So please, make sure you close it before we go into a tunnel. The guard will blow a whistle to warn you.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Some people expect the old carriages to be freezing, but they're actually steam-heated, so you can leave your heavy coats here on the coach. There's no need to rush to the platform when we arrive, either. The train won't leave until everyone in our group is on board. Oh, and photographers, flash is absolutely fine. It doesn't bother the crew at all.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Okay, let me take you along the line, stop by stop, so you know what to look out for. We start, of course, at Ashcombe. Have a good look at the station building itself while you're there. It's the original one from 1868, which makes it the oldest building on the whole railway. People often assume the signal box is older, because it looks so worn, but it was actually rebuilt after a fire in the 1920s.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: The first stop after that is Millbrook Halt. It's tiny, just one platform and a wooden bench. In fact, the train won't stop there at all unless someone asks the guard beforehand, so if you'd like to get off there, you'll need to tell him when we leave Ashcombe.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Then comes Kelsey Woods. There used to be a little café on the platform, but sadly it's closed this year while they look for a new owner. Don't let that put you off, though, because from the station there's a path through the trees to a waterfall. It's only about ten minutes on foot, and it's well signposted.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: After Kelsey Woods the line climbs quite steeply up to Brindle Junction. This is where the engine stops to take on water. It takes about fifteen minutes, so you'll have time to get off and watch the crew fill the tank. Years ago there was a picnic area beside the line here, but it was removed when the car park was built.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: The next station, Stavely, might look familiar to some of you. A few years ago it appeared in a television drama set in the 1930s. The production team even repainted the station sign to make it look older, and the volunteers liked it so much they kept it.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: And finally, at the end of the line, there's Hartfield. Apart from the afternoon tea I mentioned, there's a farm shop just outside the station that sells cheese, honey and bread, all made in the valley. If you want to take something home with you, that's the place. We'll have about an hour there before the coach picks us up for the drive back.

lines.speaker: guide
lines.text: Right, I can see the station coming up now. Make sure you've got your wristbands, and I'll see you all on the platform.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

lines.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how ants help to spread the seeds of plants. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Good morning. In the last few sessions we've looked at the ways plants spread their seeds using wind, water and birds. Today I want to turn to a partnership that's much less obvious, but surprisingly widespread: the dispersal of seeds by ants. The scientific term for it is myrmecochory, from the Greek word for ant, and it's been recorded in more than eleven thousand plant species, from tiny woodland flowers to shrubs in dry grasslands.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: So how does it work? The seeds of these plants carry a small attachment called an elaiosome. It's usually pale and soft, and it's packed with fats and proteins. At first, researchers assumed the ants were simply attracted by its food value. But it turns out there's more to it than that. The elaiosome gives off a chemical signal that's almost identical to the one produced by dead insects, which, of course, ants normally collect and carry home as food. In other words, the plant is exploiting a behaviour the ants already have.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: When a worker ant finds one of these seeds, it grips the elaiosome in its jaws and carries the whole thing back to the nest. That might be a distance of only a metre or two, but for a seed that would otherwise just drop beneath its parent, it makes a real difference.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Once the seed is inside, the adult ants don't eat the elaiosome themselves, as you might expect. Instead, they feed it to their larvae. And studies of several species have shown that colonies with access to these seeds raise heavier young and, in some cases, produce more new queens. So the ants are getting a genuine benefit from the arrangement.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: What happens to the seed itself? Well, the seed coat is too hard for the ants to bite through, and once the elaiosome has gone, there's nothing left to interest them. So they get rid of it, usually by dumping it in an underground chamber that the colony uses for waste. And this is where the plant benefits, because that chamber is full of food scraps, droppings and old cocoons, which means it's far richer in nutrients than the surrounding soil.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: There are other advantages, too. A seed lying on the forest floor is an easy meal for mice and for some kinds of beetle. Once it's buried in an ant nest, it's out of sight of these predators, and its chances of survival go up dramatically. Being moved away from the parent plant also means the young plant won't have to compete with it for light and water.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: And in some parts of the world, burial matters for another reason. In the shrublands of southern Australia and South Africa, which have an unusually large number of ant-dispersed plants, the vegetation burns every ten to twenty years. Seeds lying on the surface are destroyed, but seeds a few centimetres underground survive the fire, and many of them actually need the heat and smoke to trigger germination.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Now, all of this depends on the right ants being present, and that's where some worrying research comes in. In many places, native ants are being pushed out by invasive species, the best known being the Argentine ant. In South Africa, ecologists compared sites where native ants were still present with sites that had been taken over by Argentine ants.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: What they found was that the Argentine ants were perfectly happy to eat the elaiosomes. The difference was that they ate them where they found them. They didn't carry the seeds home, so the seeds were simply left lying on the surface, where they were eaten by mice or destroyed by the next fire.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Over several years, the sites with invasive ants had far fewer seedlings of the large-seeded shrubs. Small-seeded plants did rather better, because they don't rely so heavily on ants. So the whole make-up of the plant community was starting to change.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Climate change may be adding further pressure. Ants become active when the soil warms up in spring, while many plants release their seeds according to day length. As temperatures rise, the ants are appearing earlier and earlier, but the plants aren't changing their timing to match. Ecologists describe this as a mismatch, and if it grows, seeds may be released when the ants have already moved on to other sources of food.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: Finally, a word about how this is studied, because following a seed that's a couple of millimetres long is not easy. Early researchers simply sat and watched, which took an enormous amount of time. Some teams have tried attaching tiny radio tags, but even the smallest ones are too heavy for most ants to lift. The method that's really taken off recently is to coat seeds in a fluorescent dye, which glows under ultraviolet light. That means you can go out at night with a lamp and find exactly where the ants have taken them.

lines.speaker: lecturer
lines.text: In the next session, we'll look at a case where the relationship has gone even further, and the plant can't germinate at all without its ant partner. But for now, are there any questions?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

paragraphs.text: For most of human history, what people ate was decided largely by geography and the seasons. Fresh meat had to be eaten within days of slaughter, fruit was available only in the weeks after harvest, and anything carried over long distances had to be dried, salted, smoked or pickled first. Over roughly a hundred and fifty years, the development of refrigerated shipping broke this link between place and plate. Today a supermarket in northern Europe can sell grapes from Chile, lamb from New Zealand and green beans from Kenya on the same winter afternoon, and few shoppers stop to consider how strange that would have seemed to their great-grandparents.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first long-distance trade in cold did not involve machines at all. From the early nineteenth century, merchants in New England cut blocks of ice from frozen lakes in winter, packed them in sawdust and shipped them to ports as distant as the Caribbean and India. Some of the ice inevitably melted on the way, and on the longest routes a large part of each cargo could be lost, but enough survived to chill drinks and preserve fish in hot climates. Ice was also carried on fishing boats in the North Atlantic, so that catches could be landed in better condition. Natural ice, however, had clear limits. It could keep food only slightly above freezing point, its supply depended on a cold winter, and a cargo of meat packed in ice would not survive a voyage lasting several months.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The breakthrough came with mechanical refrigeration. During the 1870s, engineers in several European countries developed machines that worked by compressing a gas, removing the heat this produced, and then allowing the gas to expand, which made it extremely cold. Fitted into ships, such machines could keep a hold well below freezing for an entire voyage. In 1877 and 1878 a French steamer carried frozen meat from Argentina to France, and in 1882 the sailing ship Dunedin reached London from New Zealand after more than three months at sea, with a cargo of frozen mutton that was sold in good condition. The machine on board burned coal to compress air, and the crew had to keep it running day and night.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The commercial consequences were enormous. Countries with vast areas of grazing land but small populations, notably Argentina, Australia and New Zealand, could now sell meat to the crowded industrial cities of Europe. By the early twentieth century, frozen lamb and beef had become an ordinary part of the British diet. The food historian Clara Venn of the University of Halbridge argues that the change was felt most strongly by working-class families. Imported frozen meat sold at roughly half the price of fresh meat from British farms, she estimates, so that meat became a regular rather than an occasional part of their meals. British farmers, on the other hand, faced fierce competition, and many turned from raising animals for meat to producing milk, which could not yet be shipped across the world.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Fruit presented a different problem. Unlike meat, most fruit is damaged if it freezes, and bananas are especially sensitive: kept below about 13°C, they turn grey and fail to ripen properly, while if they are kept too warm they ripen and rot before reaching port. Specialised banana ships, introduced in the early 1900s, used powerful fans to circulate chilled air evenly through the hold, so that the fruit stayed green throughout the journey. On arrival, the bananas were placed in ripening rooms for several days before being sent to shops. Within a few decades, the banana had changed from an exotic luxury into one of the cheapest fruits available in Europe and North America.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The next major change was the refrigerated shipping container. From the 1960s, standard steel containers began to be fitted with their own electric cooling units, which were plugged into the ship's power supply at sea and connected to generators or mains electricity on land. Chilled food could now travel from farm to supermarket without ever being unloaded into a warmer space, and each container could be set to a different temperature. Later designs also controlled the air inside, reducing the amount of oxygen to slow down ripening. This allowed delicate produce such as avocados and soft fruit to travel by sea rather than by expensive air freight.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The effects on diet are still debated. A study by the Fenwick Institute for Food Studies found that households in its sample ate about forty different kinds of fresh fruit and vegetables over a year, compared with fewer than fifteen in similar household records from the 1930s. Supporters see this variety as a clear benefit to health. Critics, however, argue that year-round supply has weakened people's knowledge of when local foods are in season, and point out that refrigerated transport uses large amounts of energy. Venn herself is cautious: refrigerated shipping, she writes, did not decide what people wanted to eat, but it greatly widened the range of choices available to them.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Archaeologists working on land rarely find a site that records a single moment. Towns are occupied for centuries, rubbish pits are dug into older layers, and buildings are repaired, extended and demolished, so that objects from many periods end up mixed together. A shipwreck seems to offer something quite different. When a vessel sinks, everything aboard, from cargo and equipment to the personal possessions of crew and passengers, is lost at the same instant. For this reason wrecks have often been described as 'time capsules': sealed records of life on a particular day. Yet, as many specialists now point out, both establishing when that day was and deciding what the record actually shows are far less straightforward than the phrase suggests.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most traditional way of dating a wreck is through the objects found on it. Coins are particularly valuable, because many carry the name of a ruler or even the year in which they were minted, while pottery styles can often be placed within a span of a few decades. Such finds do not date the sinking directly, however. A ship carrying a coin minted in 1640 cannot have sunk before 1640, but it may have gone down many years later, since coins often remained in use for generations. The newest datable object on board therefore gives only the earliest possible date of the loss, and researchers look for several independent objects that point to the same period.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: A second line of evidence lies in the ship itself. Many wooden vessels were built from oak, and the width of the annual growth rings in a timber reflects the weather in each year of the tree's life. By matching the sequence of wide and narrow rings against reference records built up from thousands of samples, specialists can identify the year in which each ring formed. If the outermost ring beneath the bark survives, the year in which the tree was felled can be fixed exactly. Because ring patterns also vary from region to region, the method can show where the timber grew: the Swedish researcher Lena Holmqvist used it to demonstrate that a ship found off the coast of Poland had been built from oak felled in western France. Nevertheless, such dates must be interpreted with care. Shipbuilders sometimes reused timbers from older vessels, and a well-maintained ship might sail for thirty or forty years, so the age of the wood is not the date of the wreck.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Where objects are few and the timber is poorly preserved, archaeologists may turn to radiocarbon dating. Living things absorb carbon, including a small amount of a radioactive form that decays at a known rate after death, so measuring what remains in a piece of rope, a seed or a scrap of leather indicates roughly when the organism died. The method is most useful for very old wrecks, for which no written records or detailed pottery sequences exist. Its weakness is precision: results usually carry a margin of error of several decades, which is of little help to a historian trying to decide which of two recorded storms sank a particular ship.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Interpretation raises further problems. The time-capsule image assumes that a wreck stays as it was at the moment of sinking, but the seabed is rarely so still. Currents and storms scatter lighter objects, wood-boring creatures consume exposed timbers, and fishing nets drag material across the site. Later objects can also arrive: an anchor lost by another ship a century afterwards may come to rest among the remains. The maritime archaeologist Tomás Arriaga has argued that every wreck should be treated as the product of two histories, the ship's life before it sank and the site's life afterwards, and that the second is often as long and eventful as the first. Many wrecks were also partly salvaged soon after they sank, so the most valuable items may be missing altogether.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even when a site is well preserved, deciding what the objects mean is a matter of judgement. Cargo may say little about the people who sailed with it: a ship loaded with Chinese porcelain was not necessarily Chinese, and many merchant vessels carried crews from several countries. Personal items are often more revealing. On the wreck at Kessel Bank in the Baltic, a team led by Holmqvist found that the cargo consisted largely of English cloth, but the cooking pots, dice and religious medallions in the crew's quarters suggested that most of those aboard came from the southern Netherlands. Olive stones and fig seeds found in the galley indicated that the ship had taken on supplies at a southern European port during its final voyage.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, the usual response to such complexity was full excavation: objects were raised, cleaned and studied in laboratories. Excavation, however, is expensive and destroys the arrangement of the site as it proceeds, and waterlogged wood or iron brought to the surface must be treated for years to prevent it from cracking or crumbling. Increasingly, therefore, archaeologists record wrecks where they lie, using photogrammetry, which builds accurate three-dimensional models from thousands of overlapping photographs, and raise only selected objects. Not everyone is persuaded. Some researchers argue that wrecks left on the seabed will continue to deteriorate and may be looted, and that recording the surface reveals little about what lies buried beneath it. The debate reflects a wider shift in the discipline: a wreck is no longer seen as a treasure chest to be emptied, but as a complex record whose meaning depends on how carefully it is read.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Not long ago, boredom was something to be avoided, apologised for or cured. Today it has a growing number of defenders. A steady stream of books, podcasts and newspaper columns assures us that boredom is a hidden source of creativity, that children who are never bored will never learn to think for themselves, and that the remedy for an age of endless digital entertainment is to rediscover the empty afternoon. The appeal of this message is easy to understand, and parts of it are true. But the case for boredom, as it is usually made, rests on a confusion between the feeling itself and the circumstances in which it sometimes occurs, and once the two are separated, boredom looks considerably less valuable than its champions claim.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Part of the difficulty is that boredom, in its modern form, is a surprisingly recent idea. The noun did not come into common use in English until the nineteenth century, and the cultural historian Margit Solberg has argued that the experience it names became widespread only when industrial work and regular leisure divided people's days into periods of obligation and periods of nothing in particular. Writers on boredom often look further back, to the medieval monks who struggled against acedia, a heavy listlessness thought to strike in the middle of the day and draw them away from prayer. The comparison is tempting but loose. For the monks, acedia was a spiritual failing, a turning away from God; it was not a neutral psychological state, and certainly not one that anyone imagined might do them good.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The most serious argument for boredom's usefulness comes from psychologists who treat it as a signal. On this account, the mind continually weighs what it is doing against what else it could be doing, and boredom is the unpleasant feeling that arises when the comparison comes out badly. This much I accept: it explains why boredom is so common in meetings and queues, and why it vanishes the moment something better appears. But an alarm tells us that something is wrong, not what to do about it. An experiment by Ruth Adeyemi at Calder University illustrates the problem. Volunteers left alone in a bare waiting room were offered, halfway through, either a book of challenging logic puzzles or a simple tablet game in which they tapped falling shapes. Those who rated themselves as most bored were the most likely to choose the game, and they did not afterwards report feeling any less bored. Boredom pushed them to change what they were doing, but towards whatever was nearest and easiest.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: What, then, of creativity? The familiar stories, of the scientist whose great idea arrived as she gazed out of a train window or the novelist inspired while washing the dishes, are usually offered as evidence for the value of boredom. Yet what they describe is not boredom but mind-wandering: the drifting of thought during undemanding activity, which is frequently pleasant. The distinction matters. Jonas Petersen of the Ostmark Institute asked several hundred adults to record their thoughts and mood at random moments over a fortnight. New ideas most often followed periods of drifting thought accompanied by a relaxed mood; moments of boredom, by contrast, were filled mainly with irritation and clock-watching. What the champions of boredom really value, it seems, is idle time, and boredom is merely what idle time feels like when it goes badly.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The costs of boredom are clearest where it cannot be escaped. As automation spreads, more people are employed not to do a job but to watch a machine do it. The human-factors researcher Hana Morikawa spent two years observing signalling staff on a regional rail network and found that warnings were most often missed not during busy periods but during long, quiet stretches when nothing required attention. The staff themselves tended to blame tiredness, but the lapses occurred as often at the start of a shift as at the end, which tiredness cannot explain. Morikawa's recommendation is not that operators should learn to find their boredom useful, but that the work should be redesigned to include occasional meaningful tasks. Similar arguments apply to classrooms, where students who report frequent boredom tend to achieve less.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Defenders of boredom have one further argument, which deserves to be taken seriously. Children, they say, must learn to tolerate boredom, because adult life contains a great deal of it and the ability to endure dull but necessary tasks is part of self-control. There is something in this. A child who has never had to wait without entertainment may well find it harder, later, to sit through a long examination. But this is an argument for tolerating boredom, not for valuing it. We teach children to sit calmly through an injection, and we are right to do so; nobody concludes that injections are good for them in themselves.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: My conclusion is not that boredom is worthless. As a signal it is often accurate, and ignoring it, whether by forcing ourselves through work that has stopped making sense or by smothering it with distraction, means losing useful information. But a signal is not a cure, and the movement to celebrate boredom has made the mistake of treating the alarm as though it were the fire escape. What deserves protection is unstructured time, in which minds can wander pleasantly; what deserves to be reduced, wherever possible, is the needless boredom of badly designed jobs and lessons. We should listen to the alarm, but there is no reason to keep setting it off on purpose.

options.text: Challenging puzzles are an effective way to relieve boredom.

questions.prompt: What did Petersen's study suggest?

options.text: People think of more ideas when they record their thoughts regularly.
Boredom and mind-wandering tend to happen at the same time of day.
New ideas were linked more to relaxed mind-wandering than to boredom.
Most adults find periods of idle time unpleasant.

explanation.correct: D: new ideas followed drifting thought with a relaxed mood, while bored moments brought irritation and clock-watching.

distractors.why_wrong: Recording thoughts was the study's method, not a finding about creativity.

The study does not say most people find idle time unpleasant; boredom is what idle time feels like 'when it goes badly'.

evidence.quote: New ideas most often followed periods of drifting thought accompanied by a relaxed mood

to suggest that boredom is less painful than people believe
to illustrate how medical settings can cause boredom

explanation.correct: F: we teach children to endure injections but 'nobody concludes that injections are good for them in themselves', so being able to bear something does not make it valuable.

distractors.why_wrong: The writer says we are right to teach children to sit calmly through injections.
